title: AbbVie’s ABBV-295 supports monthly dosing after Phase I obesity study - AllSci
content: AbbVie presented detailed Phase I data for long-acting amylin analog ABBV-295, showing an approximately 11- to 12-day half-life that could support every-other-week or monthly dosing alongside dose-dependent weight loss. The EASD 2026 dataset included 60 participants in the multiple-ascending-dose portion of the study, with 45 receiving ABBV-295 and 15 placebo for 12 or 13 weeks. AbbVie said the findings support advancement into Phase II development for chronic weight management. ABBV-295 is a long-acting amylin analog that activates amylin and calcitonin receptors involved in appetite regulation and gastric emptying. Its non-incretin mechanism distinguishes it from GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists such as Eli Lilly's Zepbound (tirzepatide) and Novo Nordisk's Wegovy (semaglutide), while its long half-life could allow less frequent dosing than the once-weekly schedules used by those drugs. Mean weight loss ranged from 7.8% to 9.8% at Week 12 with once-weekly ABBV-295 and reached 9.7% with every-other-week dosing and 7.9% with monthly dosing at Week 13, versus about 0.3% with placebo. The results were consistent with topline findings reported in March. Interpretation is limited by the small and highly selected Phase I population, which had a mean age of 41.5 years and BMI of 29.3 kg/m² and was 88% male. ABBV-295 showed dose-proportional exposure, with a mean half-life of 10.7 to 12.3 days. No serious treatment-emergent adverse events or severe gastrointestinal events were reported. Nausea occurred in 33.3% of ABBV-295-treated participants versus 20.0% on placebo, while diarrhea occurred in 20.0% versus none on placebo. The most advanced amylin competitor is Zealand Pharma and Roche's petrelintide, which entered registrational Phase III development in September 2026. AbbVie has also moved ABBV-295 into a Phase II dose-finding study in adults with obesity or overweight with comorbidities. Access the AllSci platform to explore the science behind the news.  is in the headlines after the Food and Drug Administration approved Juvmo, the drugmaker's once-daily tablet tavapadon, for adults living with Parkinson's disease. Regulators cleared the medicine for use on its own in early disease and alongside levodopa in more advanced stages, and the company expects supply to reach patients in October. The approval, reported widely earlier this week, marks a major milestone for the North Chicago-based company's neuroscience franchise. It follows the acquisition of Cerevel Therapeutics, the biotech that originally developed the molecule and that AbbVie bought to strengthen its position in brain disorders. The news arrives as the company also opens the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology Congress in Vienna with a large slate of presentations, keeping AbbVie busy on several fronts as the quarter closes. Tavapadon is a selective partial agonist of dopamine receptors, designed to provide steady stimulation of pathways that control movement. The mechanism differs from levodopa, the long-standing mainstay, and from older dopamine agonists that act more broadly. Clinical studies showed improvements in motor function and in daily activities, and the once-daily schedule may simplify regimens for patients who often juggle multiple daily pills. Convenience is a notable consideration in a disease where medication timing is crucial. Neurologists will now gauge where the medicine fits, especially in early disease when physicians try to delay levodopa, and later when motor fluctuations complicate care. Movement disorder specialists also point out that non-motor symptoms, including mood changes and sleep disturbances, affect quality of life. How the new medicine performs on these fronts in everyday use will shape physician enthusiasm over the coming months and years. Patient advocacy groups have welcomed the approval, noting that new treatment options for Parkinson's disease have been scarce for many years. Education efforts will be needed so that patients and caregivers understand the titration process and what to expect when starting therapy. AbbVie acquired Cerevel to obtain a portfolio of neuroscience candidates, with tavapadon as the lead asset. The transaction reflected a strategic push to diversify beyond immunology, where the company has long depended on Humira and then on Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Neuroscience already includes established products such as Vraylar for psychiatric conditions and Botox for neurological uses, along with migraine drugs Ubrelvy and Qulipta. Juvmo adds movement disorders to the mix. Additional candidates in the portfolio address schizophrenia, depression and other conditions, giving the company multiple shots on goal in a field where success rates have historically been low. The engine of AbbVie's recent growth has been the immunology pair of Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Skyrizi treats psoriasis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, while Rinvoq covers rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis and several other inflammatory conditions. Humira, once the best-selling drug in the world, lost exclusivity in the United States and now faces biosimilar competition. Management has said the successors would replace and then surpass the lost revenue, a claim that results have so far supported. European regulators recently approved Rinvoq for active polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children, expanding its reach into younger patients and showing the breadth of the franchise. Physicians prize the strong efficacy of both medicines, which are frequently used after earlier treatments fail. Continued label expansion, along with data showing durable results, has supported demand and helped the company reshape its revenue base away from a single blockbuster. AbbVie is presenting clinical and real-world evidence across immune-mediated skin diseases at the EADV Congress, which begins today and runs into early October. Topics include atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa and other conditions. Dermatology is a competitive area where Sanofi, Regeneron, Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson and others field powerful products. Long-term data on durability, safety and quality of life help physicians choose between mechanisms. Real-world evidence complements trial results by showing how medicines perform in everyday practice, and payers increasingly pay attention to such information when structuring coverage. Congress attendees include dermatologists, researchers and patient advocates from across Europe and beyond. Scientific sessions and poster presentations offer a chance to compare results with those of competitors, and to discuss emerging themes such as long-term remission and treatment de-escalation. AbbVie's aesthetics unit, anchored by Botox Cosmetic and Juvederm fillers, offers a different business profile from prescription drugs. Sales depend on consumer spending, which can be sensitive to economic conditions. The company has used its Allergan Aesthetics platform to expand into new products and to build a loyalty program that links consumers directly with providers. Demand for facial treatments has been resilient, though the filler segment has faced softer trends. Therapeutic uses of Botox, including migraine prevention and spasticity, provide a steadier base, giving the brand an unusual dual identity in both medicine and beauty. Competition in aesthetics comes from Galderma, Revance and Merz, alongside a growing set of new toxin and filler makers. Brand loyalty, physician relationships and consumer marketing help AbbVie defend its position in a crowded field. Oncology contributes through Imbruvica, shared with Johnson & Johnson, and Venclexta, developed with Roche. Newer assets include antibody-drug conjugates, such as Emrelis, and additional programs pursued through internal work and partnerships. This month, the company announced a multi-year collaboration with Iambic to use artificial intelligence in discovering small-molecule medicines across immunology, neuroscience and oncology. Such alliances show the industry's growing reliance on computational methods. Partnerships allow AbbVie to test new approaches without committing to full acquisitions, spreading scientific bets across multiple technologies and platforms. Emrelis, the company's antibody-drug conjugate, reflects an effort to build oncology beyond blood cancers. Early experience will indicate whether solid tumor programs can add to a franchise historically defined by Imbruvica and Venclexta. Like every large drugmaker, AbbVie confronts American pricing reform. Medicare negotiation has already touched some of its products, and the administration's voluntary agreements with other manufacturers have set expectations for the rest of the industry. Management has engaged with officials and announced substantial domestic manufacturing plans, including a first facility in North Carolina, aligning with the broader push to bring production home. Rebating practices, pharmacy benefit manager dynamics and the interplay of commercial and government coverage all shape net pricing, so headlines about list prices tell only part of the story. American equities edged higher on Wednesday, led by technology and semiconductor strength, with healthcare shares roughly flat. AbbVie traded in a narrow band as the pharmaceutical group lagged the enthusiasm for artificial intelligence names. The stock has moved in a fairly tight range over recent sessions, according to market reports, reflecting steady expectations after the Parkinson's approval and a series of regulatory updates. Quarter-end positioning may influence trading, and dividend-focused holders often keep a close eye on AbbVie, which has a long record of raising its payout. The pharmaceutical group has often served as a place for defensive positioning during volatile periods, though the current rally in technology has drawn attention away. AbbVie's steady cash generation and diversified portfolio keep the stock a fixture of large-capitalization healthcare discussions. Across the wider set of healthcare stocks, companies are racing to renew pipelines as patents expire, with neuroscience, immunology, oncology and obesity among the busiest areas. AbbVie sits at the intersection of several of them. Neuroscience has drawn renewed attention after years of disappointment, with new Alzheimer's therapies, schizophrenia drugs and Parkinson's treatments all reaching the market. Funding from large companies has picked up as science improves. Regulatory speed has also become a talking point, as the agency has cleared a steady stream of new medicines in recent weeks, contributing to an upbeat tone across the industry. In immunology, AbbVie competes with Johnson & Johnson's Tremfya, Eli Lilly's Omvoh and Taltz, Pfizer's inflammatory portfolio and Bristol Myers Squibb's Sotyktu. Rivals are developing oral and long-acting alternatives. In Parkinson's disease, established products include levodopa formulations, dopamine agonists and monoamine oxidase inhibitors, with newer entrants from Supernus, Neurocrine and others. Juvmo must earn its place in treatment sequences. AbbVie's breadth across immunology, neuroscience, aesthetics and oncology provides diversification that many peers lack, though it also requires management to juggle many priorities. Production of small-molecule tablets such as Juvmo is comparatively straightforward, and AbbVie expects to launch quickly. Biologics like Skyrizi require more complex facilities and tight quality oversight. The company has expanded plants in the United States and Europe, and announced new sites as part of its domestic commitments. Supply resilience is a priority, given past global disruptions. Commercial teams are preparing education programs for neurologists and movement disorder specialists, since a new mechanism needs clear guidance on dosing, titration and monitoring. AbbVie must manage biosimilar erosion of Humira, pricing reform, competition in immunology and uncertain uptake of new launches. Executing across numerous brands simultaneously is a demanding task. Safety monitoring of Rinvoq and similar drugs, which carry class warnings, remains under regulatory review, and any change in labeling could affect demand. The company has defended the medicine's overall profile. Neuroscience launches are notoriously hard, as physician habits are entrenched and payers may require step therapy, so early uptake for Juvmo will draw attention. Manufacturing scale, supply reliability and cybersecurity are additional concerns for a company operating a complex global network. Disruptions from weather, geopolitics or regulatory inspections can delay shipments and require swift responses from operations teams. Beyond Skyrizi and Rinvoq, AbbVie is developing next-generation immunology candidates aimed at inflammatory bowel disease, dermatology and rheumatology. Combination approaches and novel targets are both under study. The company has also acquired assets to broaden its reach, including programs in bispecific antibodies and cell-based approaches that may treat autoimmune disease at a deeper level. Management views immunology as a durable growth area, since chronic inflammatory conditions affect large populations and often require lifelong treatment. Vraylar, used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and as an add-on in depression, has become one of AbbVie's important neuroscience products. Growth has been steady as physicians gain familiarity. The Cerevel deal also brought candidates for schizophrenia and other psychiatric conditions, including a muscarinic-based approach that aims to reduce side effects seen with older antipsychotics. Competition includes Bristol Myers Squibb's Cobenfy, which introduced a new mechanism, and established generics, so clear differentiation remains vital. Ubrelvy and Qulipta serve migraine patients through oral CGRP-targeted mechanisms, giving physicians alternatives to injectable antibodies. Botox adds a preventive option for chronic migraine. Together, the products give AbbVie an unusually broad presence in migraine care, from acute relief to prevention. Coverage and formulary dynamics influence how quickly patients can access each. Direct-to-consumer advertising and patient support programs have been important for uptake in this category. AbbVie is known for a generous dividend and a long history of increases, features that make the stock a favorite among patient owners. Management balances that commitment against debt reduction and business development. Acquisitions of Allergan and Cerevel added debt, and the company has steadily paid it down as cash generation from immunology grows. Share buybacks, research spending and further transactions all compete for capital, making quarterly commentary from executives a regular point of interest. Patient support programs are integral to the business, helping people start and stay on therapy despite complex insurance rules. Nurse educators, copay assistance and digital tools are part of the offering. Medicines like Skyrizi and Rinvoq are used for years, so adherence and persistence significantly shape long-term outcomes. Real-world studies increasingly measure these factors. Regulators and payers pay attention to such data when evaluating value, and the company has expanded its evidence-generation efforts accordingly. Approvals arrive in different regions on different timelines. The European Commission's clearance of Rinvoq for children with juvenile arthritis came within days of the American Parkinson's decision, illustrating the breadth of the global regulatory workload. Filing strategies must account for local requirements on data, labeling and manufacturing. Teams in North America, Europe and Asia coordinate to keep submissions aligned. Post-approval studies and safety reporting continue after launch, and the company maintains large pharmacovigilance operations to track how medicines perform in the real world. AbbVie ranks among the largest healthcare companies in the country, and its performance influences sentiment across pharmaceuticals. Its dividend record makes it a bellwether for dividend-oriented sentiment in the group. Readers following the space will watch the dermatology data flow in Vienna, the October launch of Juvmo and further regulatory decisions. Each adds detail to the picture of a company reshaping its portfolio. Today's developments illustrate how a large drugmaker can pursue fresh ventures in neurology while defending a leading immunology position, all within a market that remains cautious and selective. AbbVie also illustrates how large drugmakers manage transitions. The company lost exclusivity on its best-selling drug yet continued to grow through newer products, a story that other manufacturers facing patent expirations study closely as they plan their own paths. title: AbbVie Stock: Buy, Sell, or Hold in October? - The Globe and Mail
content: Its new billion-dollar drugs are picking up the slack. AbbVie(NYSE: ABBV), one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, has been a reliable long-term investment. It's raised its dividend annually for 53 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King that has increased its payout for at least 50 years in a row, and a dozen of its drugs generate more than $1 billion in annual revenue. But as the 10-year Treasury yield stays above 5% -- its highest level since 2007 -- is it still smart to buy and hold this dividend stock? Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » In 2023, AbbVie lost its U.S. patent exclusivity for Humira, the blockbuster autoimmune drug that once accounted for over 60% of its sales. However, it offset that slowdown by launching two new immunology drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, in 2019. It acquired Allergan, the developer of Botox, in 2020, as well as additional companies (including ImmunoGen and Cerevel Therapeutics) to further expand its portfolio. From 2025 to 2028, analysts expect AbbVie's revenue and adjusted EPS to grow at CAGRs of 9% and 21%, respectively. That growth should be driven by its soaring sales of Skyrizi and Rinvoq, along with its new drugs from ImmunoGen (oncology) and Cervel (neuroscience). At $264 per share, AbbVie still looks reasonably valued at 16 times next year's earnings, and it pays a decent forward yield of 2.6%. It's not an exciting investment, but I'd rather buy and hold this stock in this turbulent market rather than sell it. title: 3 Healthcare Dividend Stocks Offering More Than Just Income - MarketBeat
content:
The flight toward dividend-paying stocks is an example of investors taking what the market is giving. In late September, the yield on the 10-year Treasury note climbed above 5%. That's appealing to some income investors, but it won't impress those looking for a combination of growth and income. Fortunately, the market is handing these investors several opportunities in large-cap, blue-chip stocks. Not only do these stocks offer attractive, growing dividends, but they also provide exposure to the healthcare sector, which analysts continue to see as a growth area that will persist into 2027. That optimism was rewarded on Sept. 28 when the U.S. Food & Drug Administration (FDA) approved Juvmo (tavapadon), AbbVie's once-daily pill for adults with Parkinson's disease. It's the first and only selective D1/D5 receptor agonist approved for this use. This opens the door to a potential multi-billion-dollar market in the United States. The announcement gives AbbVie a catalyst beyond its leadership in immunology. That position was enhanced by the company's $10.3 billion acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics on Sept. 3. AbbVie is part of the exclusive group of stocks known as Dividend Kings. The company is likely to increase the payout of its dividend for the 54th consecutive year before the end of the year. That dividend currently pays $6.92 per share annually. The most recent came on Aug. 24. The FDA approved Imaavy (nipocalimab) for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (wAIHA), a rare and life-threatening autoantibody disease. It's the first approved treatment for the condition. In July, the FDA granted De Novo authorization for OTTAVA, J&J's table-integrated soft tissue surgical robot. Immunology is where the story gets bigger. Stelara sales continue to decline, and investors have wondered what fills that gap. The answer is taking shape. Icotyde, approved in March, is the first oral IL-23-targeting drug for plaque psoriasis. Tremfya received a label expansion in May. On Sept. 25, it met its primary endpoints in a Phase 4 study for axial psoriatic arthritis. The pipeline reinforces the growth story. Rybrevant Faspro received Priority Review in July for head and neck cancer. Caplyta, acquired with Intra-Cellular Therapies, posted positive Phase 3 results in bipolar mania. Then there's the growing dividend. JNJ is another Dividend King that has raised its payout for 64 consecutive years. In April, it lifted the quarterly dividend to $1.34 per share. That's $5.36 annually, a yield just under 2%. The one caution is valuation. JNJ is currently trading just below its consensus price target of $275.87. Analysts rate it a Moderate Buy, but much of the good news may be priced in. For income investors, that argues for buying on pullbacks rather than chasing. Oncology remains the anchor. Keytruda Qlex, the subcutaneous version, generated $463 million in second-quarter sales. That's an early sign Merck can extend the franchise. Management also views sac-TMT as central to its oncology strategy, including in combination with Keytruda. Welireg sales jumped 67% in the second quarter. Merck is also buying growth. The company acquired Terns Pharmaceuticals to expand its hematology pipeline. It also signed a $2.13 billion exclusive global license agreement with SciBrunch Therapeutics for an oral KRAS G12D inhibitor (oncology). The pipeline also reaches beyond cancer. Winrevair sales grew 75% in the second quarter, and the FDA recently expanded its label. Remigromig also met its primary endpoint in diabetic macular edema. The $3.40 annual dividend has grown for 14 straight years and yields about 2.3%. On paper, Merck's payout ratio is a jaw-dropping 272%. That number is distorted by one-time charges tied to the Terns and Cidara deals. Based on next year's estimates, the payout ratio falls to about 35%. Analysts are buying the pipeline story. On Sept. 29, Scotiabank raised its price target to $180 from $155. HSBC, Guggenheim, and Leerink Partners all lifted targets earlier this month. MRK trades just slightly above its $145.76 consensus target, suggesting that the targets are still catching up to the stock. Before you consider Johnson & Johnson, you'll want to hear this. The company announced that results from the APEX Part B Dose-Regimen-Finding Study will be presented at the 2026 EADV Congress. The event will take place in Vienna from September 30 to October 3. The study evaluates zumilokibart as a potential treatment for adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis. AbbVie continues expanding its immunology pipeline as demand grows for therapies targeting chronic inflammatory skin conditions. The latest findings highlight improvements in skin severity and itch reduction across different dosing groups. The APEX Part B study used a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled design to evaluate zumilokibart. The Phase 2 trial included 346 adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis. Participants received low, mid, or high doses of zumilokibart or placebo during the 16-week induction period. The study measured treatment performance through the EASI-75 primary endpoint at Week 16. EASI-75 tracks whether patients achieve at least a 75% improvement in skin lesion severity. Additionally, researchers evaluated skin clearance and itch reduction through secondary measures. All zumilokibart doses showed statistically significant improvements compared with placebo in EASI 90 and EASI 100 results. The treatments also improved itch levels measured through the I-NRS4 assessment. The mid and high doses delivered stronger results across key secondary endpoints. The mid-dose regimen also showed faster improvements during the trial period. AbbVie reported greater reductions in skin severity compared with placebo at Week 1. The same dose produced improved itch reduction results by Week 2. AbbVie developed the APEX Part B study to identify the most effective dosing approach for zumilokibart. The company plans to move the mid-dose regimen into Phase 3 development. The next stage will also examine longer dosing intervals for patients. Atopic dermatitis remains a chronic condition that affects skin health and causes persistent itching. Current treatments focus on reducing inflammation, improving symptoms, and maintaining long-term disease control. AbbVie’s research aims to introduce additional options for patients requiring sustained treatment. The study also evaluated safety outcomes during the 16-week induction period. The most common treatment-related events included nasopharyngitis, headache, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory infections, atopic dermatitis, and urinary tract infections. title: AbbVie Presents Detailed Phase 1 Data for ABBV-295, a Long-Acting Amylin Analog, Demonstrating Favorable Tolerability and Pharmacokinetic Profile at EASD 2026 - Investing News Network

AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV) today announced that detailed results from the multiple ascending dose (MAD) part of its Phase 1 study evaluating ABBV-295 will be presented in a short oral presentation at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) 2026 Annual Meeting (Milan, Italy; September 28 October 2). The study evaluated the tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD) of subcutaneous ABBV-295, an investigational long-acting amylin analog, in adults with a mean body mass index (BMI) of less than 30 kgm2. These detailed results being presented are from the 60 participants in Part 2B/2C of the MAD study, who were randomized to receive ABBV-295 (n = 45) or placebo (n = 15). Participants had a mean age of 41.5 years and a mean BMI of 29.3 kg/m2, and 88% were male. ABBV-295 was dose-escalated to 4, 6, or 14 mg once weekly, 14 mg every other week, or 8 mg monthly, and administered for 12 or 13 weeks.1 ABBV-295 is an investigational therapy that represents a mechanistically distinct class from incretin-based therapies such as GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists.1,2 "As the obesity treatment landscape evolves, we remain focused on bringing forth differentiated approaches that help expand available therapeutic options for people living with this complex disease," said Primal Kaur, M.D., senior vice president, global development of immunology, neuroscience, eye care and specialty at AbbVie. "These detailed results showed meaningful weight loss alongside a half-life that could support dosing less frequently than once weekly, and they reinforce the scientific rationale for targeting the amylin pathway. We look forward to advancing ABBV-295 into Phase 2 development." Key highlights from the short oral presentation include: "Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term treatment, and the practical realities of therapy, such as how often someone has to take medication and how they feel while doing it, matter a great deal for patients to stay on treatment," said Juan Pablo Frías, M.D., Medical Director and Primary Investigator at Los Angeles Institute for Metabolic Research and study author. "In this Phase 1 study, ABBV-295 demonstrated meaningful weight loss across multiple dosing regimens and a pharmacokinetic profile supportive of further evaluation of extended dosing intervals. Together, these findings support continued development of this investigational therapy for patients." Phase 1 multiple ascending dose study of ABBV-295, a long-acting amylin analog for the treatment of obesity Wednesday, September 30, 2026; 11:45 AM–12:45 PM CEST LBA SO 07 Trials of tomorrow: new therapeutic horizons ABBV-295 is an investigational asset and has not been approved for use by global regulatory authorities. ABBV-295 is an investigational, long-acting amylin analog being developed for the treatment of obesity. Amylin, a satiety hormone, has been identified as a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of obesity given its role in activating signals to the brain that result in appetite suppression and the reduction of food intake, while also acting as an inhibitory signal to delay gastric emptying. ABBV-295 has not been approved by any health regulatory authority worldwide. The safety and efficacy of ABBV-295 have not been established. The Phase 1 clinical trial is a two-part, single-center, double-blind (within cohorts), randomized, placebo-controlled, single (Part 1) and multiple (Part 2) ascending dose study of subcutaneous ABBV-295. A total of 76 healthy adult participants were enrolled in the MAD study. In Parts 2B and 2C, participants had a BMI of 27.0 to 35.0 kg/m2. The primary objective is to assess the safety and tolerability of ABBV-295. Key secondary objectives are to characterize pharmacokinetics (PK) and to investigate pharmacodynamic effects. title: Can AbbVie’s Backing Help ADARx Win Over Biotech IPO Investors at a $1.74 Billion Valuation? - Insider Monkey

ADARx is seeking a valuation of up to $1.74 billion in its U.S. IPO, with AbbVie committing up to $100 million as investors weigh its late-stage lead drug against a still-selective biotech listing market. ADARx Pharmaceuticals is testing investor appetite for another biotech listing, targeting a valuation of as much as $1.74 billion in a U.S. IPO that could raise up to $371.9 million. The San Diego-based RNA drug developer plans to offer 21.9 million shares at between $15 and $17 apiece and list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ADRX. The offering comes with backing from AbbVie Inc. (NYSE:ABBV) has agreed to invest up to $100 million through a concurrent private placement, which ADARx said would give AbbVie a roughly 4.9% stake following the IPO. DON’T MISS: Pfizer vs. Thermo Fisher: Which Healthcare Turnaround has More Upside? That relationship between the two companies isn’t entirely new, as AbbVie paid ADARx $335 million in May 2025 as part of a research collaboration. Now, prospective shareholders have to decide whether ADARx’s pipeline and pharma backing justify a valuation approaching $1.74 billion in an IPO market that remains selective. AbbVie’s involvement is one of the clearest positives surrounding the offering. IPOX Research Associate Lukas Muehlbauer described the planned investment as external validation of ADARx’s technology, and AbbVie has agreed to invest as much as $100 million alongside the IPO after previously paying ADARx $335 million for a research collaboration in May 2025. ADARx also enters the public market with multiple programs already progressing through development. Three of its experimental drugs are in clinical testing, while another two are in advanced preclinical development. Its pipeline targets diseases involving the immune, kidney, cardiovascular, and neurological systems. Most importantly, ADARx isn’t entering the market with only early-stage programs. Its most advanced candidate, onvuzosiran, is already in late-stage testing for hereditary angioedema, a rare genetic disorder that causes sudden swelling attacks. READ ALSO: Gilead vs. Abbott: Which Dividend Healthcare Stock Offers the Better Risk-Reward? That could be particularly relevant in the current IPO environment. Muehlbauer said the reopening of the biotech IPO market remains selective, favoring companies with later-stage assets, upcoming catalysts, and exposure to areas including obesity and oncology. There are also signs that biotech IPO activity has improved from a year ago. Reuters reported that biotech offerings have broadly rebounded from year-ago levels. Electra Therapeutics recently raised $350 million in an upsized IPO, while Retension Pharmaceuticals and TRex Bio have also filed for listings. The $1.74 billion valuation still asks investors to place substantial value on a company whose drugs remain experimental. ADARx has three programs in clinical testing and two in advanced preclinical development. Even onvuzosiran, the company’s most advanced candidate, remains in late-stage testing. When assessing the IPO valuation, clinical results for onvuzosiran, ADARx’s revenue, losses, cash burn, or expected timeline to commercialization are essential to determine whether the proposed valuation is cheap or expensive. The broader IPO backdrop isn’t entirely supportive either. Reuters noted that a sharp increase in Treasury yields and higher interest rates has pushed some prospective issuers to the sidelines. And although biotech offerings have recovered from year-ago levels, Muehlbauer characterized the reopening as selective rather than broad. DON’T MISS: Gilead vs. Abbott: Which Dividend Healthcare Stock Offers the Better Risk-Reward? AbbVie’s investment should also be kept in perspective. The commitment of up to $100 million is meaningful enough for Muehlbauer to characterize it as external validation, but it does not remove the clinical-development risks inherent in ADARx’s pipeline. AbbVie’s planned stake would amount to roughly 4.9% following the IPO. ADARx is coming to market with several attributes that could help it stand out in a selective biotech IPO environment, including a late-stage lead candidate, several additional development programs, and financial backing from AbbVie Inc.. But the proposed valuation of up to $1.74 billion ultimately rests on experimental medicines whose commercial outcomes remain undetermined. For prospective ADARx investors, that leaves a relatively clear divide. AbbVie’s involvement and onvuzosiran’s late-stage status strengthen the story behind the IPO, while the absence of an approved product and the inherently uncertain path from clinical development to commercialization remain central risks as ADARx seeks as much as $371.9 million from the offering. NYSE Composite secured a European clearance for its immunology therapy in children and unveiled an artificial-intelligence-driven drug-discovery collaboration, keeping the drugmaker in focus as the shares traded near record ground. The European Commission approved Rinvoq for the treatment of children with active polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, extending the reach of one of the company's cornerstone immunology medicines into a younger patient group. The approval matters because it broadens Rinvoq into pediatric care, an area where treatment options can be limited and where regulators apply careful scrutiny. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis can carry a heavy burden for young patients and their families, and additional cleared options widen the set of tools clinicians can reach for. For AbbVie, the clearance deepens an immunology franchise that has become central to the company's story. Immunology sits at the heart of AbbVie's identity, and Rinvoq together with Skyrizi has become a pillar of growth as the company works through the long tail of competition against its former flagship. Each new indication widens the addressable population and reinforces the franchises the company is counting on to carry the business forward. AbbVie also announced a multi-year collaboration with Iambic focused on artificial-intelligence-driven drug discovery across immunology, neuroscience and oncology. The pact reflects a broader movement across the industry to fold machine-learning tools into the earliest stages of research, where computational methods can help sift vast chemical space and prioritize candidates faster than traditional approaches alone. Applying artificial intelligence to discovery has become one of the most discussed themes in the sector, echoing the wider technology rally that has lifted computing and semiconductors. Whether these tools meaningfully shorten development timelines remains a question the industry is actively testing, and collaborations of this kind mark concrete steps toward answering it. For AbbVie, the pact spans three of its core therapeutic areas. On the commercial front, AbbVie reported a quarterly result that topped consensus expectations, with revenue rising at a double-digit pace from a year earlier. The company also declared a quarterly cash dividend, continuing a distribution cadence that has been a defining feature for holders who favor steady payouts. The combination of a top-line beat and a sustained dividend helped carry the shares toward record ground. Established drugmakers frequently lean on consistent distributions to reward patient holders while their laboratories advance multiyear programs, and AbbVie has kept that tradition intact. Sustaining a payout while funding an ambitious research slate requires careful balancing of cash generation against heavy development spending, and the recent results kept that balance in view. AbbVie ranks among the most closely followed members of the broad universe of healthcare stocks, a field that spans pharmaceutical developers, biotechnology innovators, device makers and care providers. Within that universe, large drugmakers with deep immunology franchises and steady cash distributions occupy a distinctive place, and AbbVie sits squarely in that cohort as it presses its newer growth engines. As a component of the S&P 500, the company also features in the baskets that broad funds track, meaning its swings ripple through diversified portfolios well beyond dedicated healthcare vehicles. That membership underscores the reach of the name and helps explain the breadth of attention its updates attract. AbbVie's recent history has been shaped by the loss of exclusivity on its former flagship immunology medicine, a transition that many watchers viewed as a defining test. The company's response leaned on Skyrizi and Rinvoq, two newer immunology therapies that have expanded rapidly across a widening set of indications. The pediatric clearance for Rinvoq fits that arc, adding another setting to a franchise the company is counting on to offset the erosion from biosimilar competition. Managing a transition of that magnitude tests the durability of any large drugmaker, and AbbVie's ability to grow its newer franchises has been central to the market's running assessment of the name. Each new indication and each quarterly result feeds that ongoing evaluation of how well the company is navigating the shift. AbbVie also stepped into the trade-and-pricing arena, with a senior company officer testifying before the United States Trade Representative on global imbalances in how transformative medicines are priced. Testimony of this kind reflects the industry's engagement with the debates that shape its operating environment, from pricing to trade to how innovation is rewarded. Large makers routinely participate in these discussions, since the outcomes influence the terms on which they operate for years. The pricing of medicines across markets remains a contested topic, and drugmakers frequently press their case that the terms of reward shape the pace of innovation. AbbVie's participation placed it within that broader conversation as officials weigh how transformative therapies should be treated across borders. AbbVie competes across a dense field of established drugmakers and biotechnology firms pursuing overlapping programs in immunology, neuroscience and oncology. In immunology in particular, rivals advance their own therapies for autoimmune conditions, and the contest to secure additional indications shapes commercial fortunes across years. Differentiation on efficacy, safety and breadth of approved uses drives how the category divides among competitors. That combination of newer immunology franchises, a widening research base and a steady distribution keeps AbbVie among the most closely followed names across the established drug group as the market weighs its progress beyond the former flagship. content: AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for JUVMO (tavapadon) tablets to treat adults with Parkinson’s disease. The once-daily medication targets D1/D5 dopamine receptors and can be used with or without oral levodopa, a common Parkinson’s disease treatment. AbbVie reported that in the Phase 3 TEMPO-1 trial, daily-living scores improved by 1.6 points with the 5 mg dose and 1.7 points with the 15 mg dose at week 26, compared with a 0.9-point increase with placebo, while TEMPO-3 showed increased “on” time without troublesome involuntary movements. AbbVie develops medicines across several therapeutic areas, including neuroscience, immunology, oncology, and other specialty care markets. The company said sustained efficacy was observed through 85 weeks among participants continuing in an open-label extension, while commonly reported adverse events included nausea, dizziness, hallucinations, and dyskinesia when JUVMO was used with oral levodopa.
